situation: How the two match-guard positions (whole-arm guard and per-alternative guard) treat their condition.
a: R-ER: "A per-alternative guard uses truthiness, like the arm guard".
b: R-EU: "An arm guard narrows the arm body; a per-alternative guard never narrows ... one rule: a guard that gates the WHOLE arm narrows (C#'s flow analysis honours `when x is not null` the same way)".
why: The positions agree on the condition's type (truthiness) and differ only on narrowing, and R-EU states why: only a guard that gates the whole arm establishes a fact for the arm body. Candidate law: a fact narrows exactly the code it gates.

situation: Whether `== None` / `!= None` on a CLR reference type is refused.
a: R-DX: "Part 1: refuse `== None` / `!= None` on a CLR reference type with the `is None` steer".
b: R-EJ: "R-DX part 1's refusal stands with a reworded steer"; then R-ES: "`== None` / `!= None` are allowed on every .NET reference type and run the type's `==` ... ~~R-DX part 1~~ is lifted for CLR types".
why: R-ES lifts R-DX part 1 (after R-EJ had kept it with a new steer), but the R-DX row itself is neither struck nor annotated; only R-ES records the supersession. Bookkeeping finding: R-DX needs a 'part 1 superseded by R-ES' mark (part 2 on truthiness stands).

situation: How a nullable-oblivious CLR member or parameter is typed when read.
a: R-DW: "Oblivious CLR members and parameters accept `None` on write and read as `T`".
b: R-EH: "An unannotated CLR reference has UNKNOWN nullability ... stored into a slot declared `T` it is null-checked at that line ... **Supersedes the READ half of R-DW** (write half unchanged)".
why: R-EH replaces the read half explicitly; the R-DW row carries no mark of it. Bookkeeping finding (R-EH is also recorded as UNPLACED, so the superseded half may still be what the compiler does).

situation: A None test written as `x == None` on a CLR reference held in a slot declared non-null `T`.
a: R-EH: "a None test on a declared non-null reference `T` is refused".
b: R-ES: "`== None` / `!= None` are allowed on every .NET reference type and run the type's `==` ... R-EH's wider point stays in #2230".
why: R-ES admits `== None` on every .NET reference type with no exception for a declared-non-null slot, and it defers R-EH's point without saying whether `== None` counts as the 'None test' R-EH refuses. R-EJ's 'is never runs user code; == runs __eq__' could make it an operator call, not a None test, but no row says so.
missing_rule: On a declared non-null reference, say once whether `== None` is a refused None test or an admitted operator call.

situation: What `s == None` does on a Core type (frozenset) versus a foreign .NET reference type.
a: R-EW: "user programs lower `s == None` to `s is null` (#2238 @ 4fb77ebae)".
b: R-ES (#2238): "`== None` / `!= None` are allowed on every .NET reference type and run the type's `==`".
why: Both cite #2238; read with R-EJ ("the operator synthesized from `__eq__` is null-safe") a Sharpy/Core type's `== None` is a null test and a foreign CLR type's runs its own operator, so they cover different receivers. Low confidence because R-ES says 'every .NET reference type' and Core's frozenset is one.

situation: Which dropped span on the close line triggers the formatter's re-pair fact.
a: R-FR: "Arm (b) of the re-pair fact keys on a dropped span holding a quote character on the close line".
b: R-FV: "Narrow R-FR (b): a quote in the given-up span counts only if a literal is still open at the line's END".
why: R-FV narrows R-FR's arm (b); the R-FR row is not struck or annotated. Bookkeeping finding (tooling, not language).

situation: The formatter/indent-map recovery facts after a lexer error.
a: R-FK: "a lex that dropped a line holding a quote character ... marks the literal map unknown"; R-FP: "the lex that feeds the map continues past the error budget without reporting".
b: R-FU: "no edits below the opener's line while the bracket is open; lines above keep their repairs".
why: Each later row builds on the earlier one and names the rejected direction of the earlier ruling ((c) of R-FP is 'the direction R-FK rejected'); they cover different lexer facts and do not pull against each other.

situation: Which Python enum model a string-backed enum follows, for ordering versus for `==`.
a: R-PK: "Ordering on ONE string-backed enum is refused in Semantic, as CPython's plain `Enum` does."
b: R-QG: "`==` between two different STRING-backed enum types compares by value, as `StrEnum` (`True` for equal values)".
why: The same string-backed enum is a plain Enum for `<` but a StrEnum for `==`; a StrEnum in CPython orders by value, a plain Enum compares by identity, so neither model gives both answers. Neither row says why the model changes with the operator.
missing_rule: Each backing kind maps to ONE Python model (Enum, IntEnum or StrEnum) for every operator; a departure for one operator names its .NET reason.

situation: `==` between members of two different enum types, int-backed versus string-backed.
a: R-ON: "`==` between two different int-backed enum types answers `False` ... Amended at call 46 by R-QG for string-backed enums (by value, as `StrEnum`); stands for int-backed enums."
b: R-QG: "`==` between two different STRING-backed enum types compares by value, as `StrEnum` ... Amends R-ON, which stands for int-backed enums".
why: The amendment is recorded on both rows, but no row says why int-backed enums follow plain Enum (`False`) while string-backed follow StrEnum (by value); CPython's IntEnum would also compare by value. The two backing kinds get opposite cross-type answers with no stated principle.
missing_rule: Cross-type `==` on enums follows one model for both backing kinds (identity-False, or by-value for every backed enum).

situation: Which Python model an int-backed enum follows, for `==` versus ordering.
a: R-ON: "`==` between two different int-backed enum types answers `False`" (plain Enum behaviour; IntEnum would compare values).
b: R-OW: "Ordering on ONE int-backed enum type keeps .NET order, as `IntEnum` ... ordering across two enum types is refused in Semantic."
why: Int-backed enums are IntEnum for `<` within a type but plain Enum for cross-type `==`. R-OW's reason (keep the status quo .NET order) covers ordering only; R-ON gives no reason for not following IntEnum. Mirror image of the R-PK/R-QG split for string-backed enums.
missing_rule: Each backing kind maps to ONE Python model for every operator; a departure for one operator names its .NET reason.

situation: Ordering on members of one enum type, int-backed versus string-backed.
a: R-OW: "Ordering on ONE int-backed enum type keeps .NET order, as `IntEnum` ... (a) records the status quo."
b: R-PK: "Ordering on ONE string-backed enum is refused ... Rejected: (b) order by value as `StrEnum`, mirroring R-OW (one-way; there is no .NET order to keep). R-OW stands for int-backed enums."
why: R-PK states the reason: an int-backed enum has a .NET order already in use, a string-backed one has none. Candidate law: keep an existing .NET behaviour where one exists; otherwise follow CPython's plain model.

situation: Whether `is` on value-type operands can answer True.
a: R-OM: "`is` / `is not` with an operand statically typed as an enum compare by member, as CPython's singletons do".
b: R-OX: "`is` / `is not` are identity only ... value types: each operand is boxed, so the answer is always `False`, with warning SPY0465; ... an enum operand compares by member (R-OM) — the one ruled exception, CONFIRMED by the owner ...: 'enum values are singletons basically'".
why: R-OX records the enum exception and the owner's reason (enum members are singletons). Explained.

situation: Equality of two values of a type that declares no `__eq__`, asked by `==` versus by a container search or container equality.
a: R-PI: "`==` / `!=` on a type that declares no `__eq__` stays REFUSED, with one rule and one code for every spelling, wrapper and site".
b: R-PL: "a container search or container equality checks identity before `__eq__` for reference-type elements ... value types keep `Equals`".
why: R-PI promises one rule for 'every spelling, wrapper and site', yet `x in [y]` or `[x] == [y]` over such a type answers by identity (reference types) or .NET `Equals` (structs) where `x == y` is refused; neither row mentions the other. Rejected option (b) of R-PI was exactly 'reference types compare identity'.
missing_rule: An equality question about a type with no `__eq__` gets one verdict at every site: refused everywhere, or identity everywhere (with `in`/container `==` counted as sites).

situation: A comparison chain over a class without `__eq__`.
a: R-OY: "A chain link is its binary twin in every outcome ... `a == c == a` over a class without `__eq__` is SPY0402 wherever `a == c` is".
b: R-PI: "`==` / `!=` on a type that declares no `__eq__` stays REFUSED".
why: R-OY applies R-PI's refusal to chains; the two agree.

situation: When module values and class `@static` values are initialized relative to each other.
a: R-PW: "Declaration order, never dropped: a store to a module or `@static` value before its initializer is kept ... the initializer still runs at its declared position ... Across classes R-PY decides."
b: R-PY (owner: "go with option 1, C# order"): "Every class ... sweeps as a unit ... the first time it is touched, or when the module's sweep reaches its position ... module-level values keep the declaration-order sweep".
why: R-PW defers the cross-class case to R-PY, and R-PY's stated basis is C#'s per-class type initialization (A1); module values have no such per-type unit. Explained, though by pointer rather than a written principle.

situation: Two classes whose static initializers read each other's values.
a: R-PY: "Across classes today's values hold (`5 5`; `out B.q`: `1 42`)."
b: R-QA: "Two classes whose initializers read each other's values raise `NameError` whichever is touched first, including the touch order that prints correct values today. Named departure from C#".
why: R-QA carves the mutual-read case out of R-PY's C# order and names the departure (T1: no touch-order-dependent silent value). R-PY's row is not annotated with the narrowing.

situation: Whether an initialization cycle between values is a compile error or a run-time NameError.
a: R-PS: "SPY0278's 'visible cycle' is decided by a map ... Rejected: SPY0278 for const cycles only, every non-const cycle a run-time `NameError`."; R-QB: "A ring of non-const values is a compile error unless a same-module store names one of its values".
b: R-QA: "Two classes whose initializers read each other's values raise `NameError` whichever is touched first".
why: R-QA rules the run-time behaviour where the cycle reaches run time; R-PS/R-QB (and R-PZ: "SPY0278 where the compiler can see it") put the visible ones at compile time. Read together they are layered, though R-QA's row does not say its NameError is only for cycles the compiler cannot see.

situation: How a spec-silent surface where Sharpy runs a program and python3 refuses it is classified under the fidelity table.
a: R-HH: "the spec is silent on case ..., so the surface is COMPARED (programs run vs refused, spec deferring to Python)" — Python's refusal adopted.
b: R-HT: "the spec has no grammar block and is silent (fidelity-scope D5: DEVIATION until promoted)" — Sharpy keeps accepting `01`, recorded as a deviation.
why: Both are 'which programs run vs are refused' with a silent spec, and the rows read spec silence in opposite ways (silence = defers to Python vs silence = unlisted, DEVIATION). R-HH also had a host-dependence reason (T4) that could have carried it alone, but the classification premise it states contradicts R-HT's.
missing_rule: A silent spec on whether a program runs is either 'defers to python3' (COMPARED) or 'unlisted' (DEVIATION) — one reading for every such surface.

situation: Sharpy accepts something CPython refuses, and users may come to depend on the acceptance.
a: R-FA: "`hmac.new` without `digestmod` is refused ... (an implicit digest is the acceptance users come to depend on, and CPython removed it on purpose) ... a kept acceptance is the one-way direction."
b: R-HT: "(a) RECORD: a `docs/deviations.yaml` row (`leading-zero-decimal-integer` ...) ... (a) accepts a spelling users may come to depend on — a → b later breaks programs — so this is the one-way choice, taken knowingly".
why: R-FA's test refuses an acceptance users would depend on; R-HT keeps exactly such an acceptance (CPython also refuses `01` on purpose) and says it is knowingly one-way, without saying why R-FA's test does not apply. The surfaces differ (stdlib call vs literal syntax), but no row states that the distinction matters.
missing_rule: When Sharpy accepts what CPython refuses: record a deviation only if no valid CPython program changes meaning and the acceptance is harmless; otherwise refuse — for syntax and library alike.

situation: A stdlib signature whose `None` default diverges from CPython.
a: R-EV: "A CPython sentinel default becomes an overload WITHOUT that parameter ... Rejected: (a) deviation row (a silent divergence on a COMPARED surface)".
b: R-FA: "`endpos: int | None = None` stays as ONE `docs/deviations.yaml` row (the stdlib `T | None = None` convention; no valid CPython program changes meaning)".
why: Different verdicts, and the rows give the reason: R-EV's divergence changes what a valid CPython call means, R-FA's only accepts a call CPython refuses. Candidate law: a divergence that changes a valid program's meaning is fixed; a pure widening may be a deviation row.

situation: CPython's fallbacks for `in` on a class without `__contains__`.
a: R-NZ: "A user class with `__iter__` and no `__contains__` answers `in` / `not in` by iteration".
b: R-OA: "A class with only `__len__` + `__getitem__` stays refused for `in` (SPY0320); a deviation row carries the owner's reason (the index need not be an integer; an integer index need not be dense)."
why: R-OA states why the second fallback differs: `__getitem__` does not imply an integer, dense sequence protocol, while `__iter__` is exactly iteration.

situation: A `None` needle in a membership test: built-in containers versus some Stdlib types.
a: R-NV: "A `T | None` needle is accepted (`None` → `False`)".
b: R-NX: "A `None`-valued needle in `IPv4Network`, `IPv6Network`, `EmailMessage` raises `AttributeError` (rejected: answer `False` with a deviation)".
why: Neither row states the reason, but R-OS later supplies it: "only the equality scans answer `False`", a receiver with its own `__contains__` raises. Explained by a later row, not by either of these.

situation: Which exception a `None` needle raises when the receiver's `__contains__` cannot take `None`.
a: R-NX: "A `None`-valued needle in `IPv4Network`, `IPv6Network`, `EmailMessage` raises `AttributeError`".
b: R-OS: "a `None` needle into an opaque receiver whose `__contains__` / `Contains` parameter is a plain value type `T` is the principle's 'a `T | None` passed into a plain `T` raises `TypeError` at that point'".
why: R-NX follows CPython's AttributeError; R-OS (and R-OP: "a `T | None` stored or passed into it ... raises `TypeError` there") makes the boundary raise TypeError. R-OS says #2635 'lands as built', which keeps R-NX, but no row says when the Stdlib receiver's CPython exception beats the boundary TypeError.
missing_rule: A None reaching a plain-T `__contains__` parameter raises one exception type: CPython's where the receiver is a COMPARED Stdlib type, TypeError otherwise — stated once.

situation: Storing a plain `T` value into a name declared `T?`.
a: R-G: "implicit `T → T?` retired ... `Some(v)`/`None()` sole constructors ... `T?` converts implicitly in NO direction."
b: R-T: "inside a narrowing, a store to the narrowed `T?` name takes the PAYLOAD type as its slot and re-wraps".
why: Outside a narrowing `x = 5` into an `int?` needs `Some(5)`; inside one the same store is implicitly wrapped. R-T is a payload-slot rule and does not cite R-G; no row says why the narrowed position may convert when R-G says no position does.
missing_rule: A narrowed `T?` name's slot type is its payload for reads and stores alike, stated as the one exception to strict construction.

situation: A non-constant (collection, tuple, Some) default value: dataclass field versus function/lambda parameter.
a: R-A: "Dataclass collection-literal field defaults lower to per-instance initialization; never a C# default-parameter value; SPY0400 stays for function params".
b: R-R: "ONE emittable-constant-default predicate consumed by all three sites; `Some(...)` and tuple literals → SPY0401 with the `= None()` + `x ??= Some(v)` steer ... Option C (forward-overload synthesis) recorded future".
why: A field default C# cannot hold is lowered; a parameter default C# cannot hold is refused. Neither row gives the reason (plausibly: Python evaluates parameter defaults once and shares them, so per-call evaluation would change meaning), so the split is unstated.
missing_rule: A default C# cannot emit as a constant is evaluated per use where Python also evaluates per use (fields), and refused where Python shares one evaluated value (parameters).

situation: The str/repr of `defaultdict`.
a: R-BN: "`str`/`repr` renders `defaultdict(<factory>, {...})`, documented as a deviation in the collections spec."
b: R-CJ: "`str`/`repr` of EVERY Stdlib type is COMPARED, one tracker per type family: every Stdlib type with a constructor-spelled python repr implements `IRepr`".
why: R-CJ is later and says EVERY Stdlib type is compared, with no carve-out for R-BN's documented placeholder; R-BN is not marked superseded. R-BN's reason (python's `<class 'int'>` needs rung-4 name-keyed magic) still applies, so R-CJ probably means to keep it, but no row says so.
missing_rule: Stdlib reprs are COMPARED except for a part naming a runtime value with no source spelling (a factory, a function), which prints a fixed placeholder.

situation: Whether run-time exception message text must match CPython.
a: R-CE: "runtime keyword text becomes python's `KeyError: 'name'`".
b: R-CI: "Exception message text beyond the type name is DEVIATION by default ... Rejected: match every message text (unbounded ...). Relaxable later."
why: R-CI sets a default (not compared) and does not forbid matching; R-CE chose to match one text (and a KeyError's text is its key). They do not pull against each other.

situation: The E2 emitter-port plan P82: its sequencing and the `MergeFrom` disjointness rule.

b: R-LV: "P82's first tranche ran ahead of its charter slot after P80 ... (R-LK's 'after P80' superseded)"; R-MB: "`MergeFrom` is equal-value tolerant ... the issue title's and row 0's 'disjoint' wording is REWORDED here."

b: R-CN: "P21d → P21e → P21b → P21c NEXT, before P15 ... Supersedes R-BI's sequencing only"; R-GV: "R-CN's ordering is superseded (its premise is now internal to the bindings plan)".

situation: A walrus `:=` whose target is an existing `let` binding.
a: R-GV: "B5 amends R-BK (`:=` on an existing `let` is an error, never a silent shadow) ... B1–B12 ... are recorded by pointer ... and never re-asked".
b: R-LR (later): "a walrus over a `let` is decided in P21b's plan with `let`'s own semantics; until then the harness pins the cells `Unruled` and the docs keep the open-question sentence ... Rejected: ... (c) refuse now (restricts two shapes that run and agree with python)".
why: R-GV records the case as already decided (an error), and R-LR treats it as open and rejects refusing it now; R-LR does not cite R-GV/B5. R-BK ("declare-if-new, rebind-if-existing") is also not marked as amended by B5.
missing_rule: Whether `:=` onto an existing `let` is an error, a write-through, or open must be stated once; R-GV's B5 and R-LR cannot both stand.

situation: Whether a module-scope non-const binding (`x: T = e`, `let x`) is legal.
a: R-BL: "module-scope non-const bindings (`x: T = e` without keyword, `let x`) are SPY0340 with the steer 'module-scope bindings are `const`'" (R-CY likewise reasons 'dies under const-only module scope').
b: R-GV: "ruling A (module `const`-only) and the 2026-09-21 'no mutability axis' are superseded"; R-QI: "A module-level or `@static` declaration with no initializer is REFUSED ..., with a steer to `x: int = 0`" (a mutable module value, as R-PW's stores to module values also assume).
why: Later rulings treat non-const module values as legal and R-GV says the const-only rule is superseded, but R-BL's refusal and steer are not marked, and R-CY's stated rationale rests on the dropped premise. Medium because R-GV names 'ruling A', not R-BL, and the link is inferred.

situation: A comprehension's walrus over an outer name that is read afterwards.
a: R-MJ: "A comprehension's walrus over a visible outer name read after it is REFUSED ... narrowed by R-MH for same-function bindings."
b: R-MH: "a comprehension's walrus over a binding of the SAME function — a local or a parameter — writes through as python does ... this narrows plan-3eba57 D9 (R-MJ), which stays in force for a module or enclosing outer."
why: Both rows record the narrowing. The remaining split (same-function writes through, module/enclosing refused) matches N6's same-function store rule, so it is explained by law, though the N5 text in name-resolution.md still says 'ruling open on #2427'.

situation: Membership in `bytes` with an `int` needle versus a `bool` needle (an int in Python).
a: R-NU: "`bool` and `decimal` needles into `range` and `bytes` stay refused (SPY0222); the stated reason is the implicit-conversion rule".
b: R-NW: "A `bytes` container takes a `bytes` needle (subsequence) and an `int` needle (one byte)".
why: R-NU gives the reason: Sharpy has no implicit `bool` → `int` conversion, so a bool needle does not fit the int slot.

situation: Truth-testing a fixed-arity tuple versus a `tuple | None`.
a: R-AU: "A fixed-arity tuple is not truth-testable by the spec's own rule (no falsy case ...) ... `tuple | None` keeps the null test".
b: R-OB: "The truth value of a `T | None` is python's — `None` or a falsy payload is false — in every truth-testing position".
why: R-AU's reason (a type with no falsy value is not truth-testable) explains why `tuple | None` (falsy when None) is testable and `tuple` is not; R-OB's rule gives the same answer for a non-empty fixed-arity payload. Candidate law: a type is truth-testable only if it has a falsy value.

situation: A warning on using a `T | None` without narrowing it.
a: R-Z: "Closed by design (loose family per spec + #882) ... opt-in unnarrowed-deref warning filed as parked #1793."
b: R-OV: "Two warning codes: one for an operation on a `T | None` that fails on `None` (member, index, iteration, `len`, arithmetic, ordering) ... default-on".
why: R-OV turns the parked opt-in warning of R-Z into a default-on one; R-Z (loose access accepted) otherwise stands under R-OP. R-Z's row is not annotated.

situation: Ordering on a `T | None` operand.

b: R-OP: "Supersedes the ordering half of R-OC".
why: Properly marked on both rows.

situation: The type of a conditional or display whose branches/elements differ.

b: R-W: "One element/branch type rule = C#'s best-common-type ... Supersedes R-B and R-L's join half ... the compiler never invents an ancestor."
why: Marked on all three rows.

situation: Bare class-body reads outside methods and forward static reads.
a: R-JJ: "C#'s rule PER POSITION ... SUPERSEDED as the governing rule 2026-11-01 by the name-resolution principle"; R-JT: "a FORWARD static read ... is refused ... SECOND HALF SUPERSEDED 2026-11-01 (N3 ...)".
b: R-KD places the N1–N7 plans that carry the replacing rules.
why: Both earlier rows carry their supersession notes in-row. Properly marked.

situation: A bare class-body name read inside a lambda in a class-body initializer, and inside a nested type.
a: R-JV: "a lambda in an initializer reads what its ENCLOSING initializer may read ... SUPERSEDED 2026-11-01 (N1; R-KF, R-KG): a lambda is a body — class-body names stay invisible bare inside it".
b: R-KG: "(a) REFUSED with a steer naming the position ... N1's list of bodies where class-body names are invisible bare gains 'nested type bodies' beside methods, nested functions, lambdas".
why: R-JV is struck and annotated; R-KG and R-KF are consistent with the replacing N1 rule.

situation: Collisions of an import binding with another module binding.
a: R-II: "An import alias is checked like every other module binding: a same-module class/def/alias collision is SPY0204".
b: R-IZ: "an explicit import of a different source COLLIDES with a star-exported name in both orders — SPY0204 at the explicit import ... python3 is last-wins ... the spec rules (R-II's precedent)."
why: R-IZ extends R-II's collide-by-rule principle to star imports; they agree.

situation: Where the value-ness work (enums and struct-like types as value types) is planned.
a: R-NY: "Enums are value types across the compiler ... a third `/verify-plan` pass on plan-4e2867 is allowed."
b: R-OQ: "Supersedes the placement of R-NY and of R-OO only; the work itself is not dropped — R-OU rules it."
why: R-OO records the move in-row; R-NY does not. Bookkeeping finding (placement, not semantics).

situation: A numeric literal that its type cannot represent: overflow versus underflow, float versus decimal.
a: R-HU: "REFUSE every numeric literal outside the range of its own resolved type ... CPython: `1e400` is `inf`. Rejected: (b) float64 unsuffixed → `inf` ... `x: float = 1e400` then carries infinity into arithmetic silently".
b: R-IA: "A non-zero `decimal` literal whose value becomes zero is REFUSED ...; float32 and float64 keep IEEE underflow to zero (C#'s and CPython's value) ... Rejected: (c) refuse non-zero→zero for every float type (refuses `print(1e-400)`, which CPython runs printing `0.0`)".
why: The rows give the reasons: float underflow keeps the value C# and CPython agree on; float overflow (C# refuses, CPython gives inf) and decimal underflow (C# silently 0m) are refused. Candidate law: an unrepresentable literal is refused unless C# and CPython give the same value.

situation: A class-level (static) member reached through `self`: store versus read.
a: R-KU: "(a) REFUSE with the steer 'write `H.x = …`' — python's meaning (an instance / subclass attribute: `2 5`) cannot be matched".
b: R-LQ: "`self.N()` on a nested type is ADMITTED, lowered type-qualified `C.N()` — one rule for class attributes read through `self`".
why: R-KU says why the store differs: in Python a store through `self` creates an instance attribute, which Sharpy cannot match, while a read through `self` has the same meaning as the qualified read. Candidate law: admit a spelling only where its Python meaning is kept.

situation: `str()` of a value of a built-in union type: Optional versus Result.
